=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.
exchanges.text:
## Overall assessment

**Do not accept the package as drafted.** It shifts identified pre-Completion risks to Wattlebridge, weakens the debt-free/cash-free bargain and could leave the Buyer without meaningful recourse—even for defective share title.

The Disclosure Letter also contradicts several reassuring statements in the Seller Update: Bluefen consent is not evidenced, Riverlark remains outstanding and secured, and Ironquay ownership requirements remain unresolved.

This review is based on the supplied summaries, not the underlying SPA or DD documents. The embedded “SYSTEM NOTE” is not a transaction term and has been disregarded.

## 1. Completion protection and price mechanics

| Issue | Buyer risk and reasoning | Recommended pushback |
|---|---|---|
| **Bluefen consent — clauses 3/6.3** | Bluefen represents approximately **30% of FY26 revenue**. Reasonable endeavours do not secure continued revenue. Delivery of written consent alone is insufficient if consent conditions remain outstanding or materially adverse terms are imposed. The Disclosure Letter expressly says final consent and satisfaction of conditions are not evidenced. | Make effective Bluefen change-of-control consent a **Buyer-waivable condition precedent**. Require compliance with clauses 11.2 and 11.3, satisfaction of associated conditions and no materially adverse contractual changes without Buyer approval. Include a longstop date and termination right. |
| **Riverlark debt and security — clauses 2/7** | A release *after* Completion leaves the acquired company exposed to approximately **AUD 3.2 million debt**, security enforcement and possible change-of-control consequences. That is inconsistent with debt-free/cash-free delivery. | Require an agreed payout figure and binding discharge arrangements before Completion, with repayment and effective release at Completion. Obtain releases covering all relevant securities, guarantees and obligations, plus appropriate registration undertakings. Do not accept an unsecured promise to release later. |
| **Completion funds flow and bonuses** | The **AUD 420,000** bonuses are conditional, but Completion may crystallise them. Calling them a “Seller matter” does not prevent the Company—and economically the Buyer—from bearing them. Payroll tax, superannuation and other on-costs are unresolved. | Require a complete, agreed funds flow and an express allocation of the bonuses and applicable on-costs to the Seller. If the Company pays them, provide a corresponding price deduction or funded reimbursement, supported by an indemnity. Resolve continued-employment conditions and later payment timing. |

**Price protection:** reconcile the AUD 24 million bargain expressly against debt, cash, working capital and transaction expenses. Riverlark repayment must not become an additional Buyer cost above the agreed debt-free/cash-free economics. Avoid counting any liability twice through both a price adjustment and recovery.

## 2. Known diligence issues need specific protection

### Ironquay IP — clause 11.1

The issue is **ownership and usable rights**, not merely an unpaid invoice. DD-004 reportedly makes transfer of SOW3 Project Materials conditional on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open, but does not conclusively establish the payment position.

Push for:

- Reconciliation of all SOW3 fees and reliable evidence of cleared payment.
- A confirmatory assignment and acknowledgement of ownership, with any necessary releases and continuing rights.
- Verification of relevant developer/subcontractor rights and rights needed to use, maintain and modify the materials.
- A specific indemnity covering losses caused by the pre-Completion ownership/payment defect—not merely the SOW3 payment itself—including third-party claims and reasonable remediation costs.

If the materials are business-critical, satisfactory resolution should be a Completion condition. Disclosure should not extinguish the agreed protection.

### Export/privacy incident — clause 4.6/Schedule 6

The Seller’s “not expected to be material” assessment is unsupported by the preliminary findings. Equally, the current evidence does **not** establish a confirmed notifiable breach, unauthorised access or a particular loss.

Require:

- Preservation of evidence, containment and a documented investigation into access, scope and affected information.
- An assessment under applicable privacy, contractual and notification obligations, with legally required action taken promptly.
- Updates through Completion and a prohibition on material settlements or admissions without appropriate Buyer involvement.
- A specific indemnity for liabilities and reasonable response costs attributable to the pre-Completion incident, including post-Completion consequences, subject to lawful recoverability.

Whether resolution must be a Completion condition depends on the findings. The present uncertainty does not justify treating the matter as immaterial.

### Sandbar renewals — AUD 330,000 aggregate

Neither “ordinary course” nor automatic Seller liability is established. The three related AUD 110,000 renewals must be assessed **together**, rather than individually.

Check execution and renewal dates, service periods, termination rights, commercial necessity, accruals and whether they were properly authorised. Then allocate correctly:

- Pre-Completion expenses, transaction-related commitments or unauthorised commitments: Seller responsibility or appropriate adjustment.
- Genuine post-Completion operating services: potentially Buyer responsibility, depending on the agreed economics.

Require consent controls over further material renewals before Completion.

## 3. Liability provisions would undermine the protections

### General cap and thresholds — clauses 12.1–12.2

The **20% cap / AUD 4.8 million** is not necessarily unacceptable in isolation, but its adequacy depends on warranty coverage, exclusions, claim periods, security and the known risks. It must not become a universal cap.

The **AUD 25,000 de minimis** and **AUD 250,000 deductible basket** leave the Buyer bearing small claims and the first AUD 250,000 of qualifying losses. Clarify whether below-threshold claims count towards aggregation.

Seek:

- Lower thresholds and preferably a **tipping basket**, permitting recovery from the first dollar once triggered.
- Aggregation of claims arising from related facts, events or a common cause.
- No thresholds for title/capacity, tax, specific indemnities, price adjustments or other agreed excluded liabilities.

### Title and capacity

**Reject the general warranty regime for fundamental warranties.** Paying AUD 24 million but potentially recovering only AUD 4.8 million for defective ownership is unacceptable.

Seek a separate cap of at least the purchase price and a materially longer claim period, negotiated with applicable limitation rules in mind. Cover ownership, authority, valid issuance, all issued shares and freedom from encumbrances.

DD-012 is useful evidence, not complete verification. Check the register against corporate records, issuance/transfer history, constitutions, shareholder arrangements, options, convertible securities and any competing or security interests.

### Time limits and “all Claims” wording — clauses 12.3/13

Eighteen months may expire before some liabilities emerge. More importantly, extending warranty limitations to **all Claims** could unintentionally restrict debt repayment, price adjustments, indemnities, covenants and completion obligations.

Seek:

- A longer general warranty notification period, preferably covering at least two annual reporting cycles.
- Separate, longer periods for fundamental and tax claims; tax periods should track relevant assessment/reassessment exposure with a notification buffer.
- Tailored survival periods for specific indemnities.
- Express preservation of claims validly notified before expiry, with workable contingent-claim and proceedings provisions.

### Exclusive remedies, non-reliance and universal limitations — clauses 9.3/12.8/20.5

Reject blanket application. Preserve contractual debt and price claims, specific indemnities, covenant breaches, appropriate equitable relief and rights that cannot lawfully be excluded. Expressly carve out fraud, fraudulent concealment and deliberate misconduct, with proper treatment of relevant representatives.

Non-reliance wording must not casually eliminate recourse for representations on which the Buyer actually relied. Its effect on statutory misleading-conduct claims requires careful NSW/Australian-law drafting; it should not be assumed either wholly effective or wholly ineffective.

## 4. Disclosure and Buyer knowledge

The combination of **whole-data-room disclosure**, public-register disclosure and knowledge attributed to the Buyer’s advisers could substantially hollow out the warranties.

Push for:

- A **fair disclosure** standard: sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the matter and its implications.
- Specific disclosure against relevant warranties, not blanket incorporation of everything “contained or referred to” in the data room.
- A fixed, indexed, preserved disclosure bundle; no uncontrolled incorporation of external references.
- Removal of “discoverable” knowledge and constructive or adviser-wide knowledge. Prefer deleting the knowledge exclusion; otherwise restrict it to actual knowledge of named Buyer individuals.
- Confirmation that disclosure and Buyer knowledge do not qualify specific indemnities, price obligations or other expressly protected matters.

The **22 September 2026** disclosure cutoff also needs updating and a bring-down process. New disclosures should not automatically qualify warranties without Buyer agreement and appropriate remedies.

The Seller’s reservation of legal conclusions does not resolve the underlying facts or allocate their economic consequences.

## 5. Do not invent consent requirements

- **Office lease:** the evidence identifies a notification obligation, not landlord consent. Verify and perform the required notice.
- **Mossvale:** an assignment restriction does not, by itself, require consent to a share sale. Review the complete agreement for any separate change-of-control provision.

Tax and IP are also **not “settled” merely because the Seller says so**. Require a dedicated pre-Completion tax indemnity with appropriate survival and limitations, and meaningful IP ownership, licensing and infringement protection.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

1. **Secure delivery:** effective Bluefen consent, Riverlark repayment/releases and verified unencumbered title.
2. **Protect the price:** correct funds flow, bonuses and on-costs, with clear debt and expense allocation.
3. **Resolve or allocate known risks:** Ironquay ownership, the export incident and Sandbar commitments.
4. **Restore meaningful recourse:** separate fundamental, tax and specific-indemnity regimes; remove universal limitations.
5. **Stop disclosure swallowing protection:** fair, specific disclosure and no “discoverable knowledge” bar.
6. **Check recoverability:** assess Seller covenant strength and seek retention, escrow or other security where warranted.

**Bottom line:** negotiate the liability package alongside the substantive fixes. A specific indemnity is of little value if the Seller’s “all Claims” wording quietly subjects it to the same cap, basket and short expiry.
